lead: The transport layer lets many applications share a single host. It does this by assigning a 16‑bit port number to each process. The pair (IP address, port) is called a socket address; a socket is the tuple (IP address, port, transport protocol). The operating system reads the port in every incoming segment and delivers the payload to the correct application. This mechanism is called multiplexing at the sender and demultiplexing at the receiver. It is used for web browsing, video streaming, online payments and any client‑server communication on the Internet.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 (layering) and Unit 4 (IP addressing).

blocks.text: A port number identifies a transport endpoint on a host. It is an unsigned 16‑bit integer, so the range is 0 ≤ port ≤ 65535. Values 0‑1023 are well‑known ports reserved for standard services such as HTTP (80) and DNS (53). Values 1024‑49151 are registered ports used by applications. Values 49152‑65535 are dynamic or private ports assigned temporarily by the OS.

blocks.where: 2¹⁶ is the number of distinct values a 16‑bit field can hold

blocks.text: A socket is the tuple (IP address, port number, transport protocol). The protocol part distinguishes UDP from TCP when the same port number is used by both.

items: Port 0 is reserved; it is not used as a destination port in normal communication, but it may be used as a source port to request an OS‑assigned ephemeral port or as a wildcard in certain socket APIs.
Port numbers are stored in network byte order (big‑endian).
The OS maintains a table mapping each active port to a process identifier (PID).

blocks.text: When an application sends data, the transport layer attaches the source and destination ports to the segment. This is multiplexing because the same physical link can carry segments for many applications simultaneously.

items: Application calls sendto() with destination IP and port.
Transport adds source port (chosen by OS) and destination port.
Network layer encapsulates the segment in an IP packet.
Link layer transmits the frame on the medium.

blocks.text: At the receiver, the OS extracts the destination port from the incoming segment. It looks up the port in its socket table. If a match is found, the payload is copied to the buffer of the owning process. This is demultiplexing.

items: If no process owns the port, the OS discards the segment and may send an ICMP “port unreachable”.
Both UDP and TCP use the same port field for demultiplexing, but TCP also uses the connection tuple (source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port).

blocks.text: Some textbooks call a socket an endpoint, a service access point (SAP), or a demultiplexer. The term “transport service” refers to the set of operations offered to the application, such as reliable byte stream (TCP) or best‑effort datagram (UDP).

items: Service Access Point – emphasizes the role of the port as an access point to the transport service.
Demultiplexer – the function that selects the correct process based on the port.

examples.question: Host A runs App 1 on port 5000 and App 2 on port 5001. Host B runs App 3 on port 6000 and App 4 on port 6001. App 1 sends a 120‑byte UDP datagram to App 3. Show how the OS on Host B processes the incoming packet and state which process finally receives the payload.
steps: The IP packet arrives at Host B and is handed to the UDP module.
UDP reads the destination port field, which is 6000.
The OS looks up port 6000 in its socket table and finds it bound to App 3 (process ID 3124).
UDP removes its header and copies the 120‑byte payload into the receive buffer of process 3124.
App 3 reads the buffer and obtains the 120‑byte message.

traps: Mistaking the port number for the IP address of the host.
Assuming that a port number is unique across the entire Internet; it is only unique per host.
Confusing the source port with the destination port when tracing a packet flow.

quiz.q: What is the size of the port field in the TCP and UDP headers?
Explain why two different applications on the same host can use the same transport protocol without interfering with each other.
quiz.a: Each application is bound to a distinct port number. The OS uses the port to demultiplex incoming segments, delivering each segment to the process that owns the matching port.

quiz.q: A server listens on TCP port 8080. A client sends a SYN packet from source port 34567. Identify the four‑tuple that uniquely defines this TCP connection.
quiz.a: The tuple is (client IP, 34567, server IP, 8080).

quiz.q: If a UDP datagram arrives with destination port 53, which standard service is it usually intended for?
Host X receives a TCP segment with destination port 0. What will the OS do and why?
quiz.a: Port 0 is reserved and cannot be used as a destination port. The OS will drop the segment and usually respond with a TCP RST (reset) segment, not an ICMP ‘port unreachable’ message.

quiz.q: Name two alternative terms for a socket used in some syllabi.
Why does the OS store port numbers in network byte order?
quiz.a: Network byte order (big‑endian) is a common convention for all Internet protocols, ensuring that hosts with different native byte orders interpret the port field consistently.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern cloud platforms, port allocation is managed by orchestration tools such as Kubernetes, which map container ports to host ports dynamically. Research on port randomization aims to reduce the risk of port‑scanning attacks. Future curricula may cover multiplexing across multiple transport protocols simultaneously, e.g., QUIC using UDP ports. Search for “socket API security” and “dynamic port allocation in microservices” for deeper insight.
